# docs/manual/agent-quickstart.md

# Cicada quick start for agents

Cicada turns a text score into audio. A command that takes `--json` prints one
JSON document on standard output, on success and on failure: decide from it and
the exit status (0 is success).

## The loop

1. Start: `cicada new demo` makes the project folder `demo` with a song in
   `main.cicada`. Run every other command inside `demo`.
2. Write: replace `main.cicada` with your score (next section).
3. Check: `cicada check --json main.cicada`. Go on when `valid` is true.
   `scores[0].revision` is what your next edit must send.
4. Render: `cicada render main.cicada -o mix.wav --loudness -14 --json`. Go on
   when `ok` and `loudness.target_met` are true.
5. Listen: `cicada audition main.cicada --json`.
6. Edit: put intents in `edit.json`, preview with
   `cicada apply main.cicada edit.json --json`, then add `--write`. Go on when
   `ok` and `written` are true; repeat from step 3.

Step 1 prints:

<!-- agent-example: new demo -->

```text
demo/main.cicada
```

<!-- agent-example-folder: demo -->

## The score

Eight bars, three tracks:

<!-- agent-example-file: main.cicada -->

```cicada
cicada 2
tempo 120
key a minor

track drums drums {}
track bass acid { cutoff = 700Hz }
track keys piano { octave = 3 level = -8dB }

pattern beat drums {
  bd: X... .... X... ..x.
  sd: .... X... .... X...
  ch: x.x. x.x. x.x. x.xx
}
pattern line { 1 . 1 . 5, . 1 . 1 . 1 . 3 . 5, . }
pattern chords { [1 3 5] - - - - - - . [6, 1 3] - - - - - - . }

scene verse { drums = beat bass = line keys = chords }
scene drop { drums = stop bass = line keys = chords }
song { verse*4 drop*2 verse*2 }

fx ceiling limiter { ceiling = -1dBTP }
master { insert = ceiling }
```

- Start every score with `cicada 2`. Outside a project, a score without it is
  edition 1, and some edits are refused.
- `track <name> <voice> { settings }`. Voices include `drums`, `acid`, `piano`,
  `fm_bass` and `poly_keys`. Values carry units.
- A pattern is 1 to 64 steps and repeats; 16 steps fill one bar. `.` is a
  rest, `-` holds the note before it, `|` only groups steps.
- `1` to `7` are degrees of the key's scale; `'` raises one an octave and `,`
  lowers it; they sound in the track's `octave` (default 2). `a1` and `c#3`
  are absolute (C4 is MIDI 60). `[1 3 5]` is a chord, except on `acid`, which
  plays it as three fast notes.
- A drum pattern has one row per lane (`bd sd ch oh cp rs lt mt ht cb cy`), all
  the same length: `x` hit, `X` accent, `.` silence.
- A scene gives each track a pattern (`stop` silences it). `song` plays scenes
  in order: `verse*4` is four bars of `verse`.
- The last two lines are a master limiter. Keep them (mistake 1).

<!-- agent-example: check --json main.cicada -->

```json
{"schema": "cicada.check.v1", "valid": true, "scores": [
  {"file": "main.cicada", "valid": true,
   "revision": "310f3c57244d24e1cf9eaf3e7185a80ff284c8a83af140b3901552fc07a15e32"}]}
```

## Hearing the result

<!-- agent-example: render main.cicada -o mix.wav --loudness -14 --json -->

```json
{"schema": "cicada.render.v1", "ok": true,
 "loudness": {"target_lufs": -14, "target_met": true}}
```

<!-- agent-example: audition main.cicada --json -->

```json
{"schema": "cicada.audition.v1", "score": {"written_key": "A minor"},
 "heard_key": [{"key": "A minor"}], "harmony_mismatches": 0, "tracks": [
  {"id": "drums", "masked": false},
  {"id": "bass", "masked": true, "level_vs_loudest_db": -27.9}]}
```

- Too quiet: `tracks[].masked` (buried in the mix), or `level_vs_loudest_db`
  far below 0: here the bass is 27.9 dB under the drums.
- Too bright or dull: `tracks[].centroid_hz`; higher is brighter.
- Silent: `tracks[].silent`, or a bar in `bars` whose `match` is `silent`.
- Out of key: `heard_key[0].key` differs from `score.written_key`, or
  `harmony_mismatches` counts bars whose `match` is `disagree`.
- Clipping: `target_met` includes a true peak at or below
  `true_peak_max_dbtp`. Without `--loudness`, `levels.clipped_count` must be 0.
- `--from <bar> --bars <n>` limits `render` and `audition` to some bars.

## The envelope

A batch is checked whole and written as one revision, or not at all:

<!-- agent-example-file: edit.json -->

```json
{"version": 1, "revision": "310f3c57244d24e1cf9eaf3e7185a80ff284c8a83af140b3901552fc07a15e32", "intents": [
  {"kind": "setparam", "entity": "param:bass.level", "value": "6dB"},
  {"kind": "setparam", "entity": "param:drums.level", "value": "-10dB"},
  {"kind": "replacedeclaration", "declaration": "pattern", "name": "line",
   "text": "pattern line { 1 . 1 . 5, . 1 . 1 . 3 . 5 . 1' . }"}
]}
```

<!-- agent-example: apply main.cicada edit.json --write --json -->

```json
{"schema": "cicada.apply.v1", "ok": true, "written": true,
 "revision_after": "157ddfb89b2ad22a8ce78f68ca2e0a8d65881efeb189390352474943261b9c2c"}
```

- `revision` is the SHA-256 of the score file in hex. Always send it: apply
  refuses (`revision_mismatch`) if the file changed since.
- Without `--write`, apply writes nothing and returns the `diff`.
- `entity` names what an intent changes: `param:<track>.<control>`,
  `pattern:<name>`, `step:<pattern>/<index>` (from 0), or on drums
  `step:<pattern>/<lane>/<index>`.
- When no intent fits, `replacedeclaration` replaces one declaration
  (`declaration` is `pattern`, `track_decl`, `scene_decl` or `song_decl`) and
  `replacetext` the whole score (`source`).

## Reading a refusal

A refusal exits non-zero; `apply` and `render` give `error` with a stable
`code` (branch on it) and a `message`.

- `check`: each of `scores[].diagnostics` has `code`, `message`,
  `start.line`, `start.column`, often a `hint`, and sometimes a `fix` whose
  `intents` you apply with `fix.revision`.
- `apply`: `error.code` is <!-- apply-error-codes -->`intent_refused`,
  `invalid_result` (the result does not check), `revision_mismatch`, `decode`,
  `read`, `write` or `usage`<!-- /apply-error-codes -->. `error.index` (from
  0), `error.kind` and, when known, `error.field` name the intent at fault, and
  `error.reason` a stable code for why. Nothing is written; resend the batch.
- `render`: `error.code` names the cause. A missed target still writes its
  best try, and `loudness.integrated_lufs` and `true_peak_dbtp` say what it
  reached: with no `remedy`, aim there or lower.

## Three mistakes to avoid

1. A loudness target with no master limiter: the song `cicada new` writes
   fails at -14 LUFS with `loudness_shortfall_at_true_peak_ceiling`. Way out:
   apply `error.remedy.intents` (the limiter) with `remedy.revision` and
   `--write`, then render again. The project then fails
   `check --profile browser`, as a browser image cannot carry a master insert
   yet; for the browser, keep the target at or below the error's
   `loudness.integrated_lufs`.
2. Reusing a revision after a write: `revision_mismatch`. Way out: send
   `revision_after` from the last apply, or run `check --json` again.
3. Guessing a name or a control: `apply` exits 1 with `intent_refused` and a
   message such as `unknown pattern "lines"` (`field` is `entity`) or
   `track keys does not expose sound parameter "cutoff"`. Way out: names from
   `symbols --json`. For a control, take a `path` from `cicada params` whose
   `voices` hold the track's engine (`fm_bass` is `fm`, `poly_keys` is
   `analog`, others their own name) and confirm it with `cicada explain`,
   which fails for a control the track lacks. `level` and `pan` fit any track.

## Look things up

- `cicada intents --json --index`: every kind and its meaning.
- `cicada intents --json <kind>`: a kind's fields and examples.
- `cicada symbols --json <score>`: the names a score defines.
- `cicada explain <score> <track>.<control>`: a control's value.
- `cicada params`: controls, with engine, unit and range.
- `cicada diagnostics --json <code>`: a code's meaning and fix.
- `cicada help --json <command>`: a command's usage and flags.

# docs/manual/agents.md

# Agents and JSON output

An agent can run the whole loop from the command line and read every result as
JSON: discover the commands, learn the edit intents, check a score, edit it,
render it to a loudness target and listen to it. This page describes each JSON
format, with an example that the binary produced.

The `--json` formats share these rules:

- Every run with `--json` prints exactly one JSON document on standard output,
  on success and on every failure, a usage error included. Warnings,
  diagnostics as text and error messages go to standard error.
- Every document has a `schema` field that names its format and version, in
  the form `cicada.<format>.v<version>`, such as `cicada.check.v1`. A field is
  added in a compatible way; a change that would break a reader gets a new
  version. `cicada audition --json` also keeps its older `format` field
  (`cicada.audition/1`) beside `schema` (`cicada.audition.v1`).
- Keys are snake_case. Lists whose order has no meaning are sorted, and no
  document carries a timestamp. The one older format outside these rules is
  `cicada symbols --json`: a list of symbols without a schema, whose positions
  use the keys `Line` and `Column`.
- Paths follow one rule in every document: a path inside the working folder is
  relative to it, with forward slashes (`sub/song.cicada`); a path outside it
  is absolute.
- A failure carries an `error` object with a stable `code` and the `message`
  the command prints. `check` also reports `valid` false, and its diagnostics.
- The exit status is the same as without `--json`:

  | Command | Success | Failure | Usage error or unknown name |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `check`, `apply`, `intents`, `diagnostics`, `audition` | 0 | 1 | 1 |
  | `render`, `stems` | 0 | 1 | 2 |
  | `help`, `agents` | 0 | — | 2 |

Usage errors and unknown names have the codes `usage`, `unknown_kind`
(`intents`), `unknown_code` (`diagnostics`) and `unknown_command` (`help`).

`cicada audition --json` is described in [Audition](docs/manual/audition.md), and
`cicada verify-wav --report` in [Exporting](docs/manual/exporting.md). The loudness fields
use the names of `verify-wav --report` (`integrated_lufs`, `true_peak_dbtp`,
`clipped_count`); Studio's export report calls the integrated loudness
`achieved_lufs`.

## Reading the formats

A client that reads these documents should:

1. Check `schema` first and refuse a version it does not know: compare the
   whole string, such as `cicada.check.v1`.
2. Ignore fields it does not know.
3. Rely on this: within one version, fields are only added. A field's meaning
   or type changes only with a new version.

Every example below is checked: `make test-agent-surface` writes the files this
page shows into an empty folder, runs the commands in page order with the built
binary, and fails if a value shown here differs from the output. Long outputs
are shortened: an object may leave out fields and a list may stop early, but
nothing shown is changed.

## The example score

The examples edit this score, saved as `song.cicada`:

<!-- agent-example-file: song.cicada -->

```cicada
cicada 2
title "Agent example"
tempo 120
key a minor

track bass acid { cutoff = 620Hz }
track drums drums {}

pattern riff { a1 . c2 . e2 . a1 . a1 . c2 . g2 . e2 . }
pattern beat drums {
  bd: x... x... x... x...
  ch: ..x. ..x. ..x. ..x.
}

scene main { bass = riff drums = beat }
song { main*4 }
```

## agents --json

`cicada agents` prints the [quick start for agents](docs/manual/agent-quickstart.md): the
one page an agent that has never seen Cicada reads first. The binary carries
it, so it needs no repository checkout, and `cicada new` writes it into each
new project as `AGENTS.md`. `cicada agents reference` prints the
[core reference](docs/manual/agent-reference.md): the quick start, the language, sound and
formats in brief, and one line for every command, edit intent, diagnostic code
and effect route.

`cicada agents --json` gives the page asked for as `guide`, its name as `page`
(`quickstart` or `reference`) and its size in bytes as `guide_bytes`; in
`commands`, the commands the quick start offers for looking up the rest, each
with the `summary` of what it answers (placeholders such as `<kind>` are in
angle brackets); and in `pages`, each page the binary carries with its `name`,
`title` and `bytes`. The agent task suite reads this document and runs every
command in it.

## help --json

`cicada help --json` lists every command, sorted by name, with its one-line
summary, its usage lines and its flags. `argument` names the value a flag takes
and is absent for a switch. `cicada help <command> --json` gives one command.

<!-- agent-example: help --json -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.help.v1",
  "usage": "cicada <command> [arguments]",
  "commands": [
    {
      "name": "agents",
      "summary": "print the quick start for AI agents"
    },
    {
      "name": "apply",
      "summary": "apply typed edit intents to a score",
      "usage": [
        "cicada apply <score.cicada> <intents.json> [--write] [--json] [--author <name>] [--session <id>]"
      ],
      "flags": [
        {
          "name": "--write",
          "description": "write the validated edits (default: print a diff only)"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

## intents --json

`cicada intents` lists every edit intent that `cicada apply` accepts, with its
meaning; `cicada intents <kind>` shows one with its fields and an example. The
catalog is generated from the intent registry, so it lists every kind the
binary has.

`cicada intents --json` writes the whole catalog, and `cicada intents --json
<kind>` one kind. `envelope` describes the object that carries the intents.
For each intent:

- `meaning` is one line; `notes` adds what else the intent's documentation
  says.
- `reasons` lists the codes the intent's refusals can carry, the `reason` of
  an `apply --json` error (below). A test derives the list from the code, so
  an agent can match on it.
- Each field has its JSON `name`, its `type` (`string`, `integer`, `number`,
  `boolean`, `entity`, `object`, `array` with `items`, or `any`), whether it is
  `required`, and its `unit`, allowed `values` and `meaning` where the code
  knows them. An `entity` is a string such as `pattern:riff`,
  `step:riff/3` (steps count from 0), `step:beat/bd/0`, `param:bass.cutoff`,
  `placement:intro`, `song:0` or `setting:main/bass.cutoff`.
- `required` is true when `cicada apply` refuses the intent without the
  field. A field that is not required may be left out: it is then read as its
  zero value (0, "", false or empty), which the intent takes as the default
  its meaning states.
- `required_when` names a condition under which an optional field becomes
  required: another field of the intent has one of `values`, or, with
  `present`, is given at all. In the example below `setstep` needs
  `velocity` when its `mode` is `hit`.
- `one_of` lists groups of fields of which the intent needs at least one,
  always or only while its `when` holds. Field names in `one_of`, and in a
  condition's `field`, are dotted paths from the intent's top level; a path
  through a list, such as `notes.pitch`, names a field of each element.
- `values` is the list the intent's handler checks, so a string outside it is
  refused. A field the catalog does not list is refused too.
- `selects` marks a field that chooses the intent's mode or operation, such
  as `mode` or `op`.
- `examples` are payloads that `cicada apply` accepts: one for each value of
  every field that `selects`, the first also given as `example`. Examples name
  the entities of a small test score (track `bass`, pattern `riff`, scene
  `main`); use the names of your own score.

A test applies every example, removes each field it sets and checks that the
intent is refused exactly when the catalog says the field is required (or
required by a `required_when` or `one_of` the example meets), and replaces each
listed value with one outside the list.

<!-- agent-example: intents --json setstep -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.intents.v1",
  "envelope_version": 1,
  "envelope": [
    {
      "name": "version"
    }
  ],
  "intents": [
    {
      "kind": "setstep",
      "fields": [
        {
          "name": "entity"
        },
        {
          "name": "mode",
          "type": "string",
          "selects": true,
          "required": true,
          "values": [
            "note",
            "hit",
            "tie",
            "rest"
          ]
        },
        {
          "name": "pitch"
        },
        {
          "name": "accent"
        },
        {
          "name": "slide"
        },
        {
          "name": "ratchet"
        },
        {
          "name": "chance"
        },
        {
          "name": "velocity",
          "type": "string",
          "required": false,
          "required_when": {
            "field": "mode",
            "values": [
              "hit"
            ]
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

`editnotes` names each note in `notes` by its pitch or, in a drum pattern, its
lane, and its `velocity` operation takes a new value or a change:

<!-- agent-example: intents --json editnotes -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.intents.v1",
  "envelope_version": 1,
  "envelope": [
    {
      "name": "version"
    }
  ],
  "intents": [
    {
      "kind": "editnotes",
      "one_of": [
        {
          "fields": [
            "notes.pitch",
            "notes.lane"
          ]
        },
        {
          "fields": [
            "velocity",
            "dv"
          ],
          "when": {
            "field": "op",
            "values": [
              "velocity"
            ]
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

<!-- agent-example: intents --json setpatternsettings -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.intents.v1",
  "envelope_version": 1,
  "envelope": [
    {
      "name": "version",
      "type": "integer",
      "required": true,
      "values": [
        "1"
      ],
      "meaning": "envelope format version"
    }
  ],
  "intents": [
    {
      "kind": "setpatternsettings",
      "meaning": "changes a pattern's swing, gate and transpose without changing its note text",
      "notes": "A drum pattern keeps transpose 0.",
      "fields": [
        {
          "name": "entity",
          "type": "entity",
          "required": true,
          "meaning": "the pattern, as pattern:<name>"
        },
        {
          "name": "swing100",
          "type": "integer",
          "required": true,
          "unit": "0.01 percent",
          "meaning": "swing in hundredths of a percent, 5000–7500 (50% to 75%)"
        },
        {
          "name": "gate",
          "type": "integer",
          "required": true,
          "unit": "percent",
          "meaning": "gate length, 10–100"
        },
        {
          "name": "transpose",
          "type": "integer",
          "required": false,
          "unit": "semitones",
          "meaning": "−24 to +24"
        }
      ],
      "example": {
        "kind": "setpatternsettings",
        "entity": "pattern:riff",
        "swing100": 5600,
        "gate": 60,
        "transpose": 0
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

`cicada intents --json --index` lists only each `kind` and its one-line
`meaning`, in less than a tenth of the bytes of the whole catalog, so an agent
can choose a kind before it asks for that kind in full. It is a format of its
own, `cicada.intents_index.v1`, with `index` in place of `envelope` and
`intents`. `--index` needs `--json`: `cicada intents` alone already lists each
kind with its meaning.

<!-- agent-example: intents --json --index -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.intents_index.v1",
  "envelope_version": 1,
  "index": [
    {
      "kind": "addaudiotrack",
      "meaning": "declares a new, empty audio track in an edition-2 score"
    }
  ]
}
```

## diagnostics --json

`cicada diagnostics` lists every diagnostic code; `cicada diagnostics <code>`
shows one with its fix. The [diagnostic code reference](docs/manual/diagnostics.md) is
generated from the same catalog. `severities` holds `error`, `warning` or both.
`scopes` says where the code is reported: `score` (checking a score), `command`
(a command's error), `studio` (Studio and browser responses) or `edit` (a
refused intent). `CICADA-NOTES` also lists the `reasons` its refusals carry.

<!-- agent-example: diagnostics --json slide-rest -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.diagnostics.v1",
  "diagnostics": [
    {
      "code": "CICADA-SLIDE-REST",
      "severities": [
        "warning"
      ],
      "scopes": [
        "score"
      ],
      "meaning": "a slide leads into a rest, so it has no effect",
      "fix": "slide into a note, or remove the slide"
    }
  ]
}
```

## check --json

`cicada check --json` runs the checks `cicada check` runs and reports, for each
score, whether it is valid, its `revision` and its diagnostics. Without a score
it checks the project. When `cicada.mod` lists the project's `source` files,
the project is one score: `scores` has one entry, the entry score, whose
diagnostics cover every listed file (each names its `file`) and whose
`revision` is that of the entry file alone. Otherwise each score in the project
folder is checked on its own and `scores` lists every one. `revision` is the
SHA-256 of the score file's bytes in hex, the form `cicada apply` compares with
an envelope's `revision`: put it in the next envelope for that score. It is
absent only when the score cannot be read.

Each diagnostic has its `code`, `severity`, `message` and `file`. `start` is
the position the checker reports: `line` and `column` count from 1, columns
count Unicode characters, and `offset` is the byte offset from the start of the
file. The checker reports a point, so `end` marks the end of the character at
`start`, as the language server does. `related` points at the first declaration
of a duplicate. `hint` is the advice `cicada check` prints. With
`--profile browser`, `browser_profile` lists the voices each track reserves
against the portable limits.

`fix`, where the checker knows one, is a repair: `intents` for `cicada apply`,
or a `command` to run. A fix is offered only when it is proven on the score
as it is: applying it alone removes its diagnostic and adds no other, even
when other errors remain. It holds only at `revision`, the score's revision
it was computed for: put that revision in the envelope, and check again after
applying. `cicada apply` refuses a batch that leaves the score invalid, so
when several errors have fixes, apply the fixes of one revision together in
one batch.

<!-- agent-example: check --json song.cicada -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.check.v1",
  "profile": "desktop",
  "valid": true,
  "errors": 0,
  "warnings": 0,
  "scores": [
    {
      "file": "song.cicada",
      "revision": "a62c420996d8d6468a2dd2b27ef40cd8d3ea867e5c6a53b9746d4f841dedeca2",
      "valid": true,
      "diagnostics": []
    }
  ]
}
```

A placement of a step pattern must start on a step. In `snap.cicada` it starts
at tick 100:

<!-- agent-example-file: snap.cicada -->

```cicada-invalid CICADA-ARRANGEMENT
cicada 2
tempo 120
track bass acid {}
pattern pulse { a1 . . . e2 . . . }
arrange {
  place intro bass pulse { at = 100ticks length = 1bars }
}
```

The check fails and offers the intent that moves the placement to the nearest
step:

<!-- agent-example: check --json snap.cicada exit=1 -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.check.v1",
  "profile": "desktop",
  "valid": false,
  "errors": 1,
  "warnings": 0,
  "scores": [
    {
      "file": "snap.cicada",
      "revision": "bb00827b7a0ef325edda51ba13ac8910483dd63feb59db92701fd5c7875c6852",
      "valid": false,
      "diagnostics": [
        {
          "code": "CICADA-ARRANGEMENT",
          "severity": "error",
          "message": "step pattern placement must start on a step",
          "file": "snap.cicada",
          "start": {
            "line": 6,
            "column": 3,
            "offset": 86
          },
          "end": {
            "line": 6,
            "column": 4,
            "offset": 87
          },
          "fix": {
            "summary": "move placement intro to the nearest step, tick 0",
            "intents": [
              {
                "attick": 0,
                "entity": "placement:intro",
                "kind": "moveclip"
              }
            ],
            "revision": "bb00827b7a0ef325edda51ba13ac8910483dd63feb59db92701fd5c7875c6852"
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

## apply --json

`cicada apply <score> <intents.json> --json` reports what the batch did:
`revision_before` and `revision_after` (the SHA-256 of the score's bytes),
whether the score `changed` and was `written`, the unified `diff`, any other
`files` the batch changes, and for each intent its `index` (from 0), `kind` and
the `label` the edit history records. The batch is one revision, so the diff
covers all of it. Without `--write` nothing is written.

When the batch fails, `error.code` is one of:

<!-- apply-error-codes -->
- `usage`: the arguments are wrong.
- `read`: the score or the intents file cannot be read.
- `decode`: the JSON does not match the envelope or an intent's kind.
- `revision_mismatch`: the envelope's `revision` is not the score's.
- `intent_refused`: an intent is refused.
- `invalid_result`: the edited score does not compile.
- `write`: the edit could not be written.
<!-- /apply-error-codes -->

`index`, `kind` and, where the code knows it, `field` name the intent at
fault. When an intent states why it refused, `reason` carries a stable code
from the intent's `reasons` list in `cicada intents --json`. Where they
apply, `uses` lists what still refers to the entity, `file` names another
source file of the project that holds what the edit would have to change
(an edit writes only the score it is given), and `range` gives the
`parameter`, the `value` given, `min`, `max` and `unit` of a value outside
its range (reason `value_out_of_range`). A refused `editnotes` batch also carries
`diagnostic` `CICADA-NOTES`, its `reason` and the `note` (see
[Editors](docs/manual/editors.md)). The text error names
the intent the same way: `intents[1].entity (togglestep): unknown pattern
"rif"`.

<!-- agent-example-file: bad.json -->

```json
{"version": 1, "intents": [
  {"kind": "setparam", "entity": "param:bass.cutoff", "value": "900Hz"},
  {"kind": "togglestep", "entity": "step:rif/3"}
]}
```

<!-- agent-example: apply song.cicada bad.json --json exit=1 -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.apply.v1",
  "score": "song.cicada",
  "ok": false,
  "written": false,
  "dry_run": false,
  "changed": false,
  "revision_before": "a62c420996d8d6468a2dd2b27ef40cd8d3ea867e5c6a53b9746d4f841dedeca2",
  "intents": [
    {
      "index": 0,
      "kind": "setparam"
    },
    {
      "index": 1,
      "kind": "togglestep"
    }
  ],
  "diff": "",
  "error": {
    "code": "intent_refused",
    "message": "unknown pattern \"rif\"",
    "index": 1,
    "kind": "togglestep",
    "field": "entity"
  }
}
```

The same batch with the pattern's settings instead applies and writes:

<!-- agent-example-file: edit.json -->

```json
{"version": 1, "intents": [
  {"kind": "setparam", "entity": "param:bass.cutoff", "value": "900Hz"},
  {"kind": "setpatternsettings", "entity": "pattern:riff", "swing100": 5600, "gate": 60, "transpose": 0}
]}
```

<!-- agent-example: apply song.cicada edit.json --write --json -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.apply.v1",
  "score": "song.cicada",
  "ok": true,
  "written": true,
  "dry_run": false,
  "changed": true,
  "revision_before": "a62c420996d8d6468a2dd2b27ef40cd8d3ea867e5c6a53b9746d4f841dedeca2",
  "revision_after": "b4e6d37792e21a8f001b0f4e44401e14157070748178f0cea330bf4627f2b6c7",
  "intents": [
    {
      "index": 0,
      "kind": "setparam",
      "label": "Set bass.cutoff"
    },
    {
      "index": 1,
      "kind": "setpatternsettings",
      "label": "Pattern · riff timing and transpose changed"
    }
  ],
  "diff": "--- a/song.cicada\n+++ b/song.cicada\n@@ -3,10 +3,10 @@\n tempo 120\n key a minor\n \n-track bass acid { cutoff = 620Hz }\n+track bass acid { cutoff = 900Hz }\n track drums drums {}\n \n-pattern riff { a1 . c2 . e2 . a1 . a1 . c2 . g2 . e2 . }\n+pattern riff { swing = 56% gate = 60% transpose = 0  a1 . c2 . e2 . a1 . a1 . c2 . g2 . e2 . }\n pattern beat drums {\n   bd: x... x... x... x...\n   ch: ..x. ..x. ..x. ..x.\n"
}
```

## render --json

`cicada render ... --json` describes what it rendered: each file in `outputs`
as its WAV header gives it (`sample_rate`, `bit_depth`, `encoding` `pcm` or
`float`, `channels`, `frames` and `duration_seconds`), and the bar range
(`from_bar`, `bars`). A render without a loudness target adds `levels`: the
pre-limiter peak and overs, the output peak, and the counts of samples at the
ceiling and clipped (`ceiling_count`, `clipped_count`, as `verify-wav
--report` names them), with peaks as linear full-scale values. `cicada stems ...
--json` lists every stem file, with `role` `stem:<file name>`.

With a loudness target (`--loudness`, or `--export` with a profile that sets
one), `loudness` gives the target and tolerance, the measured
`integrated_lufs`, `true_peak_dbtp` and `sample_peak_dbfs`, the
`applied_gain_db`, whether `target_met`, the passes, where the gain went
(`gain_stage`), the master limiter's gain reduction and the DC correction. A
measurement is `null` when there is none.

The search runs up to six passes and synthesizes the song only once.
`syntheses`, `replays` and `repeats` count how the `passes` got their audio,
and add up to `passes`: a synthesis renders the song in full; a replay runs
only the master stage again on the first pass's stored mix; a repeat is not
rendered, because its gain differs from an earlier pass's by less than the
renderer can show, so its audio and measurement are that pass's. `pass_log`
has one entry per pass, in order: the `gain_db` it applied, its measured
`integrated_lufs` and `true_peak_dbtp`, and `render`, which is `synthesized`,
`replayed` or `repeated` (with `same_as`, the number of the pass it repeats).
The audio and every other number are the same as when each pass synthesizes
the song. With the environment variable `CICADA_RENDER_NO_REUSE=1` every pass
does: `syntheses` equals `passes` and nothing is replayed or repeated. Use it
to check whether reuse caused a difference you see.

<!-- agent-example: render song.cicada -o song.wav --bars 2 --loudness -14 --json -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.render.v1",
  "command": "render",
  "score": "song.cicada",
  "ok": true,
  "from_bar": 1,
  "bars": 2,
  "outputs": [
    {
      "path": "song.wav",
      "role": "mix",
      "sample_rate": 48000,
      "bit_depth": 24,
      "encoding": "pcm",
      "channels": 2,
      "frames": 336000,
      "duration_seconds": 7
    }
  ],
  "loudness": {
    "target_lufs": -14,
    "tolerance_lu": 0.5,
    "true_peak_max_dbtp": -1,
    "integrated_lufs": -13.999999856123383,
    "true_peak_dbtp": -5.974329358809015,
    "applied_gain_db": 10.963850844317331,
    "target_met": true,
    "passes": 2,
    "syntheses": 1,
    "replays": 1,
    "repeats": 0,
    "pass_log": [
      {
        "gain_db": 0,
        "integrated_lufs": -24.96385084431733,
        "true_peak_dbtp": -16.938175787527175,
        "render": "synthesized"
      },
      {
        "gain_db": 10.963850844317331,
        "integrated_lufs": -13.999999856123383,
        "true_peak_dbtp": -5.974329358809015,
        "render": "replayed"
      }
    ],
    "gain_stage": "post_chain"
  }
}
```

A render that fails carries `error`, with a stable `code`, the `message` the
command prints and, when the documentation gives a fix for that cause, a
`remedy`. The codes are:

<!-- render-error-codes -->
- `usage`: the arguments are wrong.
- `unreadable_score`: the score cannot be read.
- `invalid_score`: the score has errors; `diagnostics` lists them.
- `export_settings`: the `--export` profile is unknown or cannot be applied.
- `output_exists`: the stems folder already exists.
- `sampler_memory`: the sampler packs exceed the resident PCM cap.
- `render_failed`: another render or write error; the message says which.
- `true_peak_and_dc_unmet`: no pass met the true-peak ceiling and the DC limit.
- `loudness_unmeasurable`: the render has no measurable loudness.
- `true_peak_over_ceiling`: the best pass is still above the true-peak ceiling.
- `limiter_reduction_over_maximum`: the master limiter would reduce more than 6 dB.
- `loudness_shortfall_at_limiter_maximum`: the target needs more than the master limiter's 6 dB maximum.
- `loudness_shortfall_at_input_gain_cap`: the target needs more than +12 dB ahead of the master limiter.
- `loudness_shortfall_at_true_peak_ceiling`: without a master limiter, the gain stops at the true-peak ceiling.
- `loudness_target_missed`: the best pass is outside the tolerance for another reason.
<!-- /render-error-codes -->

After a shortfall the best pass is still written and listed in `outputs`.

`remedy` has a `summary`, the `file` to change, the file's `revision` when the
render read it (the form `cicada apply` uses), and the `score_text` to put in
it: when `replaces` is set, `score_text` replaces that text, which occurs
exactly once in the file at that revision (the declaration it changes);
otherwise it goes at the end of the file. The remedy holds only while the file
is at `revision`: after any other change, render again. `intents`,
when present, makes the same change through `cicada apply`; it is absent when
no intent can. Today only `loudness_shortfall_at_true_peak_ceiling` has a
remedy: a limiter at the export's true-peak ceiling as the last master
insert. Its `intents` hold the `addeffect` intent that adds that limiter; put
them in an envelope with the remedy's `revision` and run `cicada apply
<score> <envelope> --write`. `score_text` describes the same change as text.
In an edition-1 score the intent carries `confirmupgrade`, because a mixer
write upgrades the score to edition 2, and `summary` says so; `score_text`
keeps edition 1. When the master chain already holds 16 inserts, the most it
takes, the remedy has neither `score_text` nor `intents`: `summary` says to
remove a master insert first.

This score has no master limiter, so its export to −9 LUFS stops at the
true-peak ceiling:

<!-- agent-example-file: loud.cicada -->

```cicada
cicada 2
tempo 138
key a minor
seed 4242
track bass acid { cutoff = 620Hz reso = 0.62 envmod = 0.7 decay = 380ms accent = 0.8 drive = 0.25 filter = diode }
track drums drums { bd_tune = 55Hz bd_decay = 400ms ch_decay = 60ms }
pattern bass-a { 1^ . 1~ 5 . 1 7, . | 1^ . 1'~ 1 5^ 3 1 . }
pattern beat-a drums {
  bd: X... .... X... ....
  sd: .... X... .... X...
}
scene main { bass = bass-a drums = beat-a }
song { main*4 }
fx tone eq { type = highpass frequency = 25Hz q = 0.707 }
master { level = 6dB insert = tone }
export loud { loudness = -9LUFS true_peak = -1dBTP normalize = off }
```

<!-- agent-example: render loud.cicada -o loud.wav --bars 4 --export loud --json exit=1 -->

```json
{
  "schema": "cicada.render.v1",
  "command": "render",
  "score": "loud.cicada",
  "ok": false,
  "outputs": [
    {
      "path": "loud.wav",
      "frames": 477914
    }
  ],
  "loudness": {
    "target_lufs": -9,
    "integrated_lufs": -10.862548607135627,
    "true_peak_dbtp": -1.050000030698375,
    "target_met": false,
    "gain_stage": "post_chain"
  },
  "error": {
    "code": "loudness_shortfall_at_true_peak_ceiling",
    "message": "loudness target shortfall 1.86 LU: achieved -10.86 LUFS at true-peak ceiling -1.05 dBTP (target -9.00 LUFS)",
    "remedy": {
      "summary": "add a limiter with ceiling = -1dBTP, the export's true-peak ceiling, as the last master insert, so the gain goes in ahead of it and it holds that ceiling (docs/audio/mix-chain.md, Export loudness targets): cicada apply with an addeffect intent (effectkind limiter, inserton master, settings ceiling), or the same in the score text",
      "file": "loud.cicada",
      "revision": "9a1336e210d4e6fddfde19678baf455fd45a31dbb38177789e133de2ac384d5f",
      "replaces": "master { level = 6dB insert = tone }",
      "score_text": "fx ceiling limiter { ceiling = -1dBTP }\nmaster { level = 6dB insert = tone -> ceiling }",
      "intents": [
        {
          "effectkind": "limiter",
          "inserton": "master",
          "kind": "addeffect",
          "name": "ceiling",
          "settings": {
            "ceiling": "-1dBTP"
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

The remedy is the one [the mix chain](docs/audio/mix-chain.md#export-loudness-targets)
describes. With its `score_text` in place of the master declaration, the same
export meets its target:

<!-- agent-example-file: loud-limited.cicada -->

```cicada
cicada 2
tempo 138
key a minor
seed 4242
track bass acid { cutoff = 620Hz reso = 0.62 envmod = 0.7 decay = 380ms accent = 0.8 drive = 0.25 filter = diode }
track drums drums { bd_tune = 55Hz bd_decay = 400ms ch_decay = 60ms }
pattern bass-a { 1^ . 1~ 5 . 1 7, . | 1^ . 1'~ 1 5^ 3 1 . }
pattern beat-a drums {
  bd: X... .... X... ....
  sd: .... X... .... X...
}
scene main { bass = bass-a drums = beat-a }
song { main*4 }
fx tone eq { type = highpass frequency = 25Hz q = 0.707 }
fx ceiling limiter { ceiling = -1dBTP }
master { level = 6dB insert = tone -> ceiling }
export loud { loudness = -9LUFS true_peak = -1dBTP normalize = off }
```

<!-- agent-example: render loud-limited.cicada -o loud.wav --bars 4 --export loud --json -->


## The agent task suite

`make test-agent-surface` builds `build/cicada` and runs the agent task suite
in `internal/agentsuite`. It starts as a new agent does: it reads the quick
start from `cicada agents`, runs its loop with its score and its batch, and
makes its three mistakes, each of which must be refused as the quick start
says; every command, field and refusal it relies on must be named in the quick
start. Then it copies `examples/first-acid.cicada` into an empty folder and
drives the binary the way an agent does, reading only JSON: `help --json`,
`intents --json`, `symbols --json`, `check --json`, an `apply` of two intents
built from the catalog's examples, `render --json` to −14 LUFS and
`audition --json`. It also runs the examples on this page and on the quick
start. CI runs it on every pull request; it must finish in under two minutes.

# docs/manual/writing-music.md

# Writing music

Start with one voice, one pattern, and one scene. Then add another part when
you know what the first one should do.

```cicada
cicada 2

title "Night circuit"

tempo 138

key a minor

seed 4242

track bass fm_bass {}

track drums drums {}

pattern bassline {
  swing = 54%
  gate = 58%
  1 . 1 5 . 1 7, . | 1 . 1' 1 5 3 1 .
}

pattern beat drums {
  bd: X... x... X... x.x.
  sd: .... X... .... X..x
  ch: x.x. x.x. x.x. x.x.
}

scene main {
  bass = bassline
  drums = beat
}

song {
  main*8
}
```

This score makes a short bass phrase and drum groove, binds both patterns to a
scene, and plays that scene for eight bars. Check the score before you open it:

```sh
cicada check
cicada fmt --check
```

Run those commands from the project directory. `check` validates every score
in the project. `fmt --check` reports files that need formatting without
changing them.

## Split a score into files

List the files in `cicada.mod` when patterns or instruments need their own source file:

```text
project multifile
cicada 2
entry "main.cicada"
source "main.cicada"
source "parts/patterns.cicada"
source "parts/voices.cicada"
license "MIT"
author "Cicada contributors"
```

The [multi-file example](examples/multifile/main.cicada) puts scenes and the song in `main.cicada`, a phrase and patterns in `parts/patterns.cicada`, and instruments and tracks in `parts/voices.cicada`. Every file shares the project's declarations. References can point forward or into another file without an import. Each file must contain complete declarations.

The entry loads first; the remaining sources load in sorted path order. The entry is included even without its own `source` line. Files outside the explicit list are ignored. Paths must stay inside the project, including through symlinks; use ordinary relative paths without `..`, absolute paths, or globs. `license` stores one SPDX identifier, quoted or bare. `author` stores a quoted string. Both are optional. Existing manifests with only `project` and `cicada` keep working unchanged.

Run these commands from the example folder:

```sh
cicada check
cicada fmt --check
cicada explain main.cicada bass.level @1.1.1
cicada play main.cicada
cicada render main.cicada -o shared.wav --rate 48000 --bits 24
```

A command given any listed source loads the whole project. `check` reports errors at the right file, line, and column; a duplicate also identifies the first declaration. `fmt` keeps files separate and retains comments and source spelling. To migrate an edition-1 project, use `cicada fix --all`; the command checks the complete project before writing each file and upgrading the manifest.

Multi-file migration requires atomic file exchange, available on supported Linux and Windows filesystems. It refuses before writing project files when that operation is unavailable. Editor saves made during publication cause a revision conflict and rollback. Displaced versions and their `.revision` receipts remain in the project directory so writes through already-open editor handles can be recovered. If a later command reports an external write or incomplete save in a recovery file, close other editors, compare and merge that version with the project file, then move the recovery file and its receipt out of the project directory before retrying.

The language server uses unsaved buffers alongside the other listed files. Go to definition and rename work across files. Save As copies all sources and their assets. Studio opens a multi-file project from any listed score. Its Code lens lists every source file; edits there are checked, saved and undone for each file on its own, and the other files keep their exact bytes. Grid, scene and recording edits are written to the file that owns the pattern or scene, and grid and scene edits share one project history. See [Score and history](docs/manual/studio.md#score-and-history).

## Import a library

A library packages instruments, effects, kits, phrases, patterns, samplers, presets, and audio assets for reuse. The [library example](examples/libraries/main.cicada) imports `demo/tone` from the project's `lib/demo/tone/` folder. Its manifest uses `library` instead of `project`:

```text
library demo/tone
cicada 2
source "tone.cicada"
license "MIT"
author "Cicada contributors"
engine 2
capabilities 0
```

A library needs an explicit source list, license, and author. It has no entry score. `cicada` declares its source edition; `engine` declares its minimum engine edition and defaults to the source edition. `capabilities` is an unsigned engine capability bit mask, decimal or hexadecimal, and defaults to zero. This engine supports editions through 2 and no optional capability bits. Unsupported requirements produce `CICADA-LIB-CAPABILITY`. A library cannot declare tracks, scenes, songs, score headers, buses, clips, mastering settings, exports, or live controls; these produce `CICADA-LIB-DECL`. An optional source edition marker must match its library manifest. An importing score accepts libraries from the same or an older source edition. Edition-1 effect shorthand retains its processor kind as a qualified named effect; edition-2 library source still requires an explicit kind.

In a score, import the path and use its final path component as the namespace:

```text
import "demo/tone"
track lead tone.glass {}
scene verse { lead = tone.melody }
song { verse*2 }
```

Libraries can import other libraries. Imports in all files of a project or library share that scope. A library's unqualified references select its own declarations; dependency references use the imported namespace. Dependencies are not re-exported. Names beginning with `_` are private to their library; referring to `tone._hook` from outside it produces `CICADA-LIB-PRIVATE`. Import cycles produce `CICADA-LIB-CYCLE`.

Paths use slash-separated source identifiers. `builtin` is reserved as an import namespace and as the first component of a library path; built-in drum recipes such as `builtin.ch` remain available. Modeled kit pieces such as `model.kick` need no import and work in library sources and in scores with imports. An import whose path ends in `/model`, such as `acme/model`, binds the name `model`, so `model.kick` then means that library's `kick` and the engine piece is out of reach. Avoid a library path that is `model` or starts with `model/`: kit lanes read every target that starts with `model.` as an engine piece, so `import "model"` silently selects the engine piece and a library at `model/perc` fails with `unknown modeled drum`. Resolution checks embedded `std/` libraries, the project's `lib/`, and the user library in that order. The user library is Go's per-OS user config directory plus `cicada/lib`; `$CICADA_LIBRARY` overrides it. Direct imports from it are allowed. A project pin explicitly selects its vendored copy while a user copy exists. Otherwise, if the same path exists in more than one location, two imports share the same final component, or an import namespace conflicts with a local declaration, loading fails with `CICADA-LIB-SHADOW`.

Library assets live under the library's `audio/` folder. Their source paths resolve from that library root, and their own declared audio hashes are verified as well. Source and asset paths cannot escape the library through traversal or symlinks. `cicada convert` refuses library-owned audio with `CICADA-LIB-ASSET` before writing output. Keep the score imports until asset vendoring is supported.

Run these commands from `examples/libraries/`:

```sh
cicada lib update
cicada check
cicada explain main.cicada tone.glass
cicada explain main.cicada lead.level
cicada play main.cicada
cicada render main.cicada -o library.wav --rate 48000 --bits 24
```

`cicada.sum` is generated and tool-owned. Commit it with the score. Each non-comment line contains `PATH KIND sha256:HASH`, where `KIND` is `std`, `project`, or `user`. Records sort by path and include transitive imports. The SHA-256 input starts with `cicada.library/1` and a zero byte, then the manifest, listed sources, and every regular file under `audio/`, sorted together by relative path. Each path and its exact bytes are preceded by their unsigned 64-bit big-endian lengths. Absolute roots and timestamps are excluded.

Every load recomputes the hashes. Missing pins, changed content, and changed resolution kinds produce `CICADA-LIB-HASH` at the importing file, line, and column. `check` reports them; playback and rendering refuse them. After an intended edit, run `cicada lib update demo/tone` to update that pin, or omit the path to update every imported library and remove unused pins. The command prints the old and new location kinds and hashes. A targeted update leaves dependency pins unchanged; update those dependencies explicitly or update all imports. A loose score uses `cicada.sum` in its own directory. An update scan containing loose scores from different directories is refused with `CICADA-LIB-ROOT`; run from each score directory or add a shared `cicada.mod`.

The language server completes import paths and public qualified names and goes to definitions in library source. Unsaved library changes also trigger hash diagnostics. `explain` identifies the library behind a declaration or instrument value. Project-wide formatting and notation fixes keep imported library files untouched. Notation fixes, local rename, and parameter hover retain import context for loose and independent scores too. Notation fixes stop on changed library pins. Use `cicada lib vendor` to keep imported user libraries in the project; Save As does this automatically. See [Managing libraries](docs/manual/libraries.md). Version requirements are not supported.

## Tracks and patterns

A track chooses a sound source: a built-in voice, a declared mono or poly
instrument, or an authored drum kit. The built-in voices are `drums`, the grand
`piano`, the 21 [keyboard patches](docs/manual/keys.md) such as `fm_bass` and `poly_keys`,
the [modeled percussion](docs/manual/modeled-percussion.md) instruments, and `acid`. A
pattern describes steps for that source. The scene connects a pattern to a
track by name.

The default grid uses sixteenth-note steps. A 16-step pattern fills one bar;
`step = 1/8`, `step = 1/4`, or an exact triplet division changes its resolution.
Patterns may contain 1–64 expanded steps and repeat while their scene plays. `.` is a
rest. `|` groups cells for your eyes and does not add a step.

The supported key scales are `minor`, `major`, `dorian`, `phrygian`,
`harmonic`, `pent`, `mixo`, and `blues`. Numbered pitches `1` through `7`
follow the selected scale. Letter pitches such as `c#3` name an absolute
pitch. Unnumbered letter pitches use the instrument's home octave, which
defaults to 2. MIDI note C4 is 60. An apostrophe raises a pitch an octave; a
comma lowers it. Leave a space between a letter pitch and a tie or next pitch:
write `c3 - e3`, not `c3-e3`.

Pattern settings go inside the braces before the steps. `swing` ranges from
50% to 75% and defaults to 50%; `gate` ranges from 10% to 100% and defaults
to 55%. `transpose` changes note patterns by −24 to +24 semitones. A pattern
without its own `seed` inherits the project seed. The project defaults are
130 BPM, A minor, and seed 0.

## Try the experimental guitar

Edition 2 can play the physical string and amp prototype with
`track lead guitar { experimental = on }`. It uses an experimental physical model; acoustic realism is unverified.

The [guitar riff](examples/expressive-guitar.cicada) demonstrates bends,
slides, palm mutes and clean versus driven amp settings. Render it with
`cicada render examples/expressive-guitar.cicada -o guitar.wav`, or open the
score in Studio. Native playback, the AudioWorklet and offline rendering all
run the model. `~` slides into the next pitch; a new note replucks the string.
Scene settings such as `lead.bend = 2` and `lead.damping = 0.8` change the
sounding string. Bend is in semitones and vibrato is in cents, both written
without a suffix. All six continuous controls smooth over 8 ms.

See [controls and limits](docs/spec/edition-2.md#experimental-guitar-voice).
Drive zero still has amp coloration. This voice models one string and a
generic amp; it does not emulate a measured guitar, circuit or cabinet.

## Change the tempo between scenes

A scene can set the song tempo. The change is a step on the bar line where the scene starts. In this score the first two bars play at 120 BPM and the last two at 66 BPM:

```cicada
cicada 2
tempo 120

track bass fm_bass {}

pattern riff steps=4 { 1 . 5 . }

scene main {
  bass = riff
}

scene outro {
  bass = riff
  tempo = 66
}

song {
  main*2
  outro*2
}
```

The tempo is a plain number from 20 to 300 beats per minute. It carries into later scenes until another scene sets it, so a run of short scenes with falling values gives a stepped slow-down. Playing from the start, seeking, and each pass of a looped song begin at the score's `tempo`. Synced delay times follow the tempo. The [scene-tempo example](examples/scene-tempo.cicada) steps from 120 down to 66 BPM, and `cicada midi` writes one tempo event for each step.

Scene tempo changes are steps; tempo ramps are not supported. Edition 2 also provides continuous `automate` lanes. Ordinary audio clips keep their recorded speed. In [Studio](docs/manual/studio.md), Session vocal comps with **Follow song tempo (keep pitch)** enabled are reprinted for tempo edits while preserving raw takes. Session count-in, punch recording, and comp placement follow the song's tempo map. See [scene tempo](docs/spec/edition-1.md#scene-tempo).

## Shape a note

Keep modifiers next to the note they change:

- `^` adds an accent on an `acid` track. Other voices ignore it; give them a
  `velocity:` row to vary their loudness.
- `~` slides into the next playable note. `acid`, authored synths and the
  guitar glide to the new pitch; the piano and the keyboard patches hold the
  first note until the next one starts.
- `*2` through `*8` retriggers the note that many times in one step.
- `?70` gives the note a 70% chance on each seeded pass.
- `-` ties the preceding note; `.` is a rest.

A note without `?` has a 100% chance. The legacy `%70` spelling is still
accepted; `cicada fix` changes it to `?70`.

Chance uses the pattern seed, track index, compiled pattern slot, pass number,
and step index. The same score therefore makes the same decisions in playback
and WAV export, independent of audio block size. All lanes of a drum pattern
use its compiled slot; a lane number does not replace the slot in the chance
hash. Changing a pattern's slot can change its seeded decisions.

You can reuse a phrase and transpose a use:

```cicada
cicada 2
track bass fm_bass {}
phrase hook { 1 . 1 5 }

pattern verse {
  use hook
  use hook +7
}

scene main { bass = verse }
song { main*8 }
```

Phrase uses expand before scheduling. Each use can repeat 1–64 times and
transpose by up to 24 semitones; the expanded pattern still has to fit the
64-step limit.

## Generate a starting phrase

`cicada gen` makes a deterministic bass phrase from a seed, key, and density
settings. It plays the `fm_bass` voice unless `--voice` names another, such as
`--voice piano`. Save the generated source and optional trace to separate files:

```sh
cicada gen --seed 4242 --key a --scale minor --trace -o generated.cicada > generated.trace.json
cicada check generated.cicada
```

Use a new output filename. The generator defaults to a 16-step phrase, a C
minor key, the AABA structure, and the `fm_bass` voice. It writes accents and
slides for every voice, but only `acid` sounds an accent, so
`--voice acid` is where `--accent-density` is most audible. The full option
ranges and defaults are in the
[generator reference](docs/spec/edition-1.md#phrase-generator-command).

## Write drum rows

Each drum row names one of the built-in lanes. `x` is a hit at velocity 100,
`X` is an accented hit at velocity 127, and `x1`–`x9` select stepped
velocities. `.` leaves a cell silent. Rows in one pattern must have equal
length; any lane you leave out is silent.

The built-in lanes are `bd`, `sd`, `ch`, `oh`, `cp`, `rs`, `lt`, `mt`, `ht`,
`cb`, and `cy`. An authored kit can route a lane to a custom instrument or to
its built-in recipe. See the [kit and lane reference](docs/spec/edition-1.md#authored-kits).

## Define an instrument

Use an instrument when you want a sound made from Cicada's typed synthesis
primitives. A `voice mono` or `voice poly` block has ordered `let` bindings and one audio
output. Parameters and inputs carry types and units, so a frequency cannot
silently be used where a time value is expected.

```cicada
cicada 2
instrument glassbass {
  octave = 2
  param cutoff = 720Hz
  param bite = 0.65
  voice mono {
    let osc = saw(pitch)
    let shape = env(gate, 380ms)
    out = ladder(osc, cutoff, bite) * shape
  }
}

track lead glassbass { cutoff = 900Hz }
pattern lead-a { 5 . 3 . 1 . 3 . }
scene main { lead = lead-a }
song { main*4 }
```

Graphs have at most 128 nodes and 32 stateful nodes. Scalar `voice poly` patterns
provide eight independent notes and release tails; chord patterns share four
slots. Authored `adsr` releases continue after note-off, until they finish or
a new note needs the slot. In Studio, **Instruments** offers Warm pad,
Wide strings, Poly brass, Silk pluck, Round bass, and Soft bell. Adding a patch
saves its editable graph and a new track together. Use `adsr` for sustained
amplitude and filter envelopes, `pulse` for variable-width oscillation, and
`svf` for resonant lowpass filtering. The mixer provides stereo positioning,
delay, and reverb. Polyphonic note patterns support two to four pitches in
brackets, such as `[c4 e4 g4]`, with shared articulation and ties. Studio's grid
can edit those chord pitches. Live note-take commits currently support single
notes; author chords in the grid or source instead. See
[Composing a complete song](docs/manual/composing-songs.md) for chord voicing and mixed grids.

Envelope time affects body as much as attack. `env(gate, 200ms)` is a
percussive decay that reaches about −40 dB in 200 ms while the gate is held;
note-off shortens its decay. Built-in drum `decay = 200ms` uses an exponential
time constant and reaches about −8.7 dB in that interval. Use `adsr` for
sustained keys and pads, and compare decay slopes when moving a drum recipe
between an authored graph and a built-in drum.

Use `comb(noise() * env(gate, 1ms), 1 / pitch, 0.995, 0.5)` for a plucked
string: a short noise burst excites a damped feedback loop. `1 / pitch` is
typed as milliseconds. `delay(sound, 60ms)` adds a slapback tap. Each primitive
reserves 16 KiB of ring storage, and each voice can contain at most two.
The [pluck example](examples/pluck.cicada) combines both operations;
[graph delay limits](docs/spec/edition-2.md#graph-delays-and-plucked-strings)
describe interpolation, time bounds, and current synthesis limits.

`ddsp(pitch, loudness)` renders a quantized neural reed from eight harmonics and
filtered noise. Use `env(gate, 620ms) * velocity` for linear loudness. The
[neural reed example](examples/neural-reed.cicada) runs in the native and
WASM kernels; its [model documentation](kernel/voice/ddsp/README.md)
describes the original CC0 training data, pinned weights, and validation.

The [instrument reference](docs/spec/edition-1.md#instruments-and-voices) lists
every primitive signature.

## Make an arrangement

Scenes give named patterns to any tracks they mention. A missing assignment
keeps that track's current pattern. `stop` stops a track, and `off` is an older
spelling of the same action; `keep` is an explicit no-change action. A song
plays scenes in order:

```cicada
cicada 2
track bass fm_bass {}
track drums drums {}
pattern bassline { 1 . 3 . }
pattern beat drums { bd: X... }

scene verse { bass = bassline drums = beat }
scene break { bass = bassline drums = stop }
song { verse*8 break*2 verse*8 }
```

Each song entry defaults to one bar and can last 1–999 bars. In Studio you can
launch a scene or pattern live and change the song lane without leaving the
source; the [Studio chapter](docs/manual/studio.md) explains those controls.

## Keep score files clear

Use `cicada fmt -w main.cicada` to write the canonical formatting. `cicada
fix main.cicada --check` reports whether legacy source spellings need
rewriting, even when the manifest already selects edition 2. `cicada fix
main.cicada` applies a meaning-preserving rewrite. If other edition-1 scores
share the folder, `fix` lists them and refuses the single-file change; run
`cicada fix --all` from the project folder to migrate them together. Both
commands check that the score parses and compiles. The specification lists every
[edition-1 spelling migration](docs/spec/semantic-model.md#cicada-fix-and-migrations).

The public [`examples/`](examples) directory includes grooves, keyboard
patches, custom instruments, and effect routing. The
[demo songs](examples/songs/README.md) develop those pieces into complete
forms with composition notes and editing exercises.

## Audio assets and samplers

Use edition 2 in `cicada.mod` to describe audio files, clip regions and a sampler.
Generate a complete example and its 9,644-byte mono PCM16 WAV from the repository root:

```sh
GOWORK=off go test ./testdata/audio-assets -run TestGenerateExample -args -out /tmp/cicada-audio-example
cicada check /tmp/cicada-audio-example/main.cicada
cicada fmt /tmp/cicada-audio-example/main.cicada
```

The Go test helper writes `cicada.mod`, `main.cicada`, and `audio/example.wav`.
The generated score contains the exact hash of the generated bytes. Its core declarations are:

```cicada
cicada 2
asset vocal "audio/example.wav" {
  sha256 = "528059ad119b79f269c9580505858c14d3636f77ade0e908942653e4c708f6ee"
  format = wav
  frames = 4800
  rate = 48000Hz
  channels = 1
  source = generated
}
clip vocal-a vocal { start = 10ms end = 4800frames gain = -2dB fade_in = 1ms fade_out = 2ms }
sampler vocal-hit { asset = vocal root = c3 mode = oneshot voices = 8 }
track chops vocal-hit { level = -8dB }
track vox audio { level = -6dB }
pattern hits { c3 . c3 . }
scene verse { chops = hits vox = vocal-a }
song { verse*4 }
```

`vocal-a` trims the first 10ms from a 100ms recording. Its end is the exclusive
source frame 4800. The `vox` audio track binds that clip in `verse`; the `chops`
track plays notes through `vocal-hit`. The sampler root `c3` is MIDI note 48,
with eight voices and one-shot mode. Use `mode = loop` for a whole-asset loop.

`check` hashes every asset and checks the WAV header against the declared rate,
channels and frame count. Asset paths resolve from the directory containing the
nearest `cicada.mod`, including scores in subdirectories. Exact `frames` literals
support sample editing; seconds and milliseconds must land on exact source frames.

The host prepares these assets before playback. Native playback and offline rendering support audio tracks and declared samplers; project images carry prepared PCM within the 2 MiB image limit. Streamed PCM uses a separate host reader.


## Standard libraries

Cicada embeds four MIT-licensed source libraries in its host binary. Use
`cicada lib list` to see their paths alongside project and user libraries.

| Import | Contents | Complete example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `std/synth` | `glassbass`, `nightbass`, `tymbal`, `subline`, `glass` graph instruments | [Standard synth](examples/std-synth/main.cicada) |
| `std/drums` | `kick`, `circuit-kick`, `snare`, `hat`; authored `steel` and `circuit` kits | [Standard drums](examples/std-drums/main.cicada) |
| `std/drum-machines` | `boom-kit`, `punch-kit`; original drum kits (older names `eight-oh-eight`, `nine-oh-nine` still work) | [Classic Drum Study](examples/drum-machines/main.cicada) |
| `std/fx` | `drive`, `delay`, `reverb`, `comp` defaults for inserts, sends, and bus compression | [Standard effects](examples/std-fx/main.cicada) |
| `std/presets` | `acid-squelch`, `acid-round`, `acid-bite`; built-in drum-kit `kit-tight`, `kit-roomy`, `kit-lofi` presets | [Standard presets](examples/std-presets/main.cicada) |

For a filtered bass graph from the Glassbass study:

```text
cicada 2
import "std/synth"
track bass synth.glassbass { cutoff = 680Hz }
```

For the three graph drum voices from Circuit kit, grouped into one kit:

```text
cicada 2
import "std/drums"
track beat drums.circuit {}
```

For a drive insert, delay and reverb sends, and music-bus compression:

```text
cicada 2
import "std/fx"
track bass fm_bass {
  insert = fx.drive
  send fx.delay = 0.3
  send fx.reverb = 0.35
}
bus music { insert = fx.comp }
```

For delay and reverb sends, use `mix = 1` on the effect and set the wet amount
with the track's `send` level. The `std/fx` returns already use this setting.
A lower effect `mix` adds a dry copy through the return while reducing the
delayed or reverberated sound; it can make a send seem quieter and narrower.
For an insert, use `mix` to blend the processed signal with its dry input.

Delay `pingpong = true` folds the **wet input** to mono using the average of
left and right. Its first echo starts on the left after `time`, the next echo
crosses to the right, and later echoes continue alternating. The first echo
keeps the per-channel peak of a centered source; its energy is now on one side,
so this is not a loudness-compensated stereo return. Adjust the send level to
taste. Stereo sources are folded down too: opposite-polarity, side-only audio
cancels in that wet input. Use `pingpong = false` for independent stereo echoes
that preserve the input channels. The dry signal keeps its original stereo
image in either mode. `width = 0` centers the wet echoes, while `width = 1`
retains the full left/right movement. Changing ping-pong mode fades its input
and feedback routing rather than replacing an active tail abruptly.

All four Drive shapes (`soft`, `hard`, `fold`, and `diode`) use 2× oversampling
to reduce distortion harmonics folding back into the audible range. This also
applies to soft saturation; a low tone setting alone cannot remove distortion
that has already folded into lower frequencies.

For an acid sound and a short-decay built-in drum kit:

```text
cicada 2
import "std/presets"
track bass presets.acid-squelch {}
track beat presets.kit-tight {}
```

Add patterns, a scene, and a song as in the complete examples. Track and scene
values can override preset values. `acid-round` uses a darker cutoff and square
wave; `acid-bite` uses a brighter cutoff, more resonance, and shorter decay.
`kit-roomy` extends the drum decays; `kit-lofi` lowers the kick tuning and darkens
the snare and hats. These kit presets target built-in `drums`; authored kits keep
their source graphs. See the [std README](project/std/README.md) for source
origins and import paths.

Run `cicada lib update` before the first check or render, and commit `cicada.sum`
with the score. Std imports are pinned with `kind std` and a hash of the exact
embedded manifest and source bytes. Upgrading Cicada does not rewrite the pins.
If that binary ships changed std content, `cicada check` reports
`CICADA-LIB-HASH`; playback and rendering refuse it. Review the change and run
`cicada lib update std/presets` to accept the new bytes, or omit the path to
re-pin every import. Unchanged content keeps its hash. Std source compiles on the
host and leaves the WASM audio kernel unchanged.

## Reuse values with a preset

A preset keeps a named set of values for an existing sound. Define it in your score or in an imported library:

```cicada
cicada 2

instrument glassbass {
  octave = 2
  param cutoff = 540Hz
  param bite = 0.58
  voice mono {
    out = lowpass(saw(pitch), cutoff) * bite * env(gate, 330ms)
  }
}

preset glassbass.bright {
  instrument = glassbass
  cutoff = 900Hz
  bite = 0.7
}

preset shimmer-keys {
  instrument = builtin.tine_ep
  tremolo = 0.6
  tremolo_rate = 5Hz
}

track lead glassbass.bright { bite = 0.65 }
track keys shimmer-keys { tremolo = 0.4 }
pattern melody { 1 . 3 . }
scene verse { lead = melody keys = melody }
song { verse }
```

`glassbass` must be a declared instrument. A library target can use a qualified name such as `tone.glass`. Library presets are also qualified at use: `track bell tone.soft {}`. Their source bytes are included in the library's `cicada.sum` hash, so changing a preset requires an explicit `cicada lib update`.

Values resolve in this order: registry default, instrument default, preset, track setting, scene setting. In the score above, `keys.tremolo` starts at the registry default 0, the preset raises it to 0.6, and the track setting lowers it to 0.4; a scene setting would replace all three. Run `cicada explain examples/presets/main.cicada bass.cutoff @2` to see every layer in one score: there a scene setting of 1400Hz overrides both the preset's 900Hz and the track's 1100Hz. Authored numeric parameters use their instrument defaults; they have no separate registry default. Scene settings support the engine's existing registry paths, including built-in voice and mixer parameters.

For built-in drums, target `drums` and use lane-prefixed names such as `bd_tune` and `sd_decay`. To save one lane's values, target `builtin.bd` and use `tune` or `decay`; a track using this preset resolves to the same drum track with those lane values. An authored kit can bind an authored instrument preset to a lane. Kit presets can set mixer values. Use a drums track for built-in recipe settings; kit bindings cannot change those settings yet.

For effects, use `preset warm { instrument = builtin.drive gain = 18dB mix = 0.75 }` and `fx grit warm { mix = 0.8 }`, then route the declared effect as usual. A declared effect can also supply defaults for an effect preset. An unreferenced effect used this way supplies defaults without creating a second runtime instance; a routed or scene-addressed target stays active. Existing effect instance limits still apply.

A sampler preset targets a declared sampler and can change `root`, `mode`, `voices`, and mixer values. Track settings can override those values. The asset remains the sampler's original asset. The built-in `audio` target accepts mixer values. The experimental guitar is not a score voice in this edition.

Presets cannot add DSP expressions, change routing, replace an asset, or inherit another preset. Unknown parameters, wrong types or units, out-of-range values, and a voice preset used as an effect (or an effect preset used as a track) produce typed errors with file, line, and column. Built-in bounds come from the shared registry. Authored parameters retain their declared units and must fit finite float32; authored bounds are not declared in this edition.

The language server completes preset targets and their parameters, including imported instrument parameters. `cicada fmt` preserves preset declarations; conversion to semantic JSON or generated source writes their resolved values. Try [Preset circuit](examples/presets/main.cicada) for an authored instrument preset, an acid preset, and a preset imported from the vendored examples library.

Studio's Library panel can save a track's stored values as a preset; see [Library](docs/manual/studio.md#library). You can also write the declaration in the score editor. Use the [library commands](docs/manual/libraries.md) to manage declarations in libraries.

# docs/manual/composing-songs.md

# Composing a complete song

A useful song example needs a musical idea, contrast, a return, and an ending.
Build those from a few reusable parts before adding more instruments. The
[demo songs](examples/songs/README.md) provide three different starting
points, including full render commands and focused editing exercises.

## Give each track a job

Start with rhythm, a low part, harmony, and a recognizable lead. They do not all
need to play at once. A sparse opening makes the later entrance of the groove
audible without changing the master volume.

[Neon Causeway](examples/songs/neon-causeway.cicada) uses an acid bass,
drum kit, and PM bell. [Lanterns After Rain](examples/songs/lanterns-after-rain.cicada)
adds extended keyboard chords. [Tidal Glass](examples/songs/tidal-glass.cicada)
uses two copies of one pluck instrument at different levels and pan positions.

Use the existing sound controls first. When you need an authored instrument,
scale its output to leave room for the other tracks and chords. Increasing a
voice count changes capacity; it is not a substitute for balancing the mix.

## Match pattern length to the musical phrase

The default cell is a sixteenth note. In 4/4, sixteen cells fill one bar.
`step = 1/8` makes eight cells one bar; `step = 1/4` makes four. Eighth-note
triplets, `step = 1/8t`, use twelve cells per bar. Patterns have at most 64
expanded cells, so a quarter-note grid can hold sixteen bars.

Different track grids can coexist. Lanterns has a two-bar drum groove and
four-bar chord, bass, and melody patterns. Its section lengths are multiples
of four bars, keeping their phrase boundaries together.

For chords, use a polyphonic graph instrument or a supported keyboard voice,
and declare the pattern as `notes`. Brackets on an acid pattern subdivide a
cell into a tuplet instead. This complete example plays a four-bar phrase:

```cicada
cicada 2
tempo 104
key d minor
track keys tine_ep { voices = 4 level = -6dB }
pattern harmony notes {
  step = 1/4
  gate = 85%
  [d3 f3 a3 e4] - - .
  [g3 bb3 d4 f4] - - .
  [bb3 d4 f4 a4] - - .
  [a2 c#3 e3 g3] - - .
  velocity: 84 . . . 88 . . . 82 . . . 96 . . .
}
scene main { keys = harmony }
song { main*4 }
```

Letter pitches make the chord voicing explicit. Scale degrees are convenient
for phrases that should retune with the score's key. The A7 above deliberately
uses C# as a leading note back to D; changing `key` does not retune that letter
pitch. A velocity-row dot holds its preceding value, and the row must begin
with a number. A tie holds the current chord's pitches together.

## Choose scenes or named placements

Use `song` when the form is a sequence of repeatable scenes. Start from an
opening, verse, fuller section, breakdown, return, and closing. Inspect the
arrangement's bar ranges in Studio's **Session** panel.

A scene binding selects a pattern. An omitted binding or `keep` carries the
previous selection; `off` releases it. Scene settings also carry forward.
When a scene should work as a standalone live launch, explicitly assign or
silence its tracks rather than depending on what happened before it.

Scene patterns follow the shared transport phase. A section entrance halfway
through a four-bar phrase need not restart that phrase. Align section lengths
with phrase lengths when you want their beginnings together.

Use edition-2 `arrange` when individual parts need their own starts and lengths.
Named placements restart a pattern at their own origin, and markers label the
form. Tidal Glass places its answering voice one beat after a section begins.
The placement's exclusive end is the first position outside its region.
Patterns on one track must not overlap; use another track for a simultaneous
voice. Choose one arrangement authority per score: `song` or `arrange`.
See [named placements](docs/spec/arrangement.md) for exact timing rules.

In Studio, select a placement in **Session** to edit its track, content,
start, or length. Drag blocks to move them and their right edges to resize;
use the time fields for an exact beat or triplet duration. Copy, add, remove,
and marker controls share the same revision checks and Undo as score edits.

Use **Loop section** to hear the transition and groove while arranging. Open
a placement and choose **Audition solo** to check its phrase, or **Audition in
song** to hear how it fits with overlapping parts. **Loop solo** and **Loop in
song** repeat the same range while you work. Moves, trims, and Undo follow at
the next bar or loop restart. **Loop an exact range** is useful for a pickup
or short transition. **Play full song** returns to the complete arrangement.
See [Session listening](docs/manual/studio.md#transport-and-session) for the controls.

## Develop the sound over time

Change one dimension at a time: note density, register, harmony, drum detail,
or filter brightness. Repeat a hook often enough to recognize it, then change
its answer or accompaniment. A breakdown can remove the rhythmic anchor while
keeping the hook, making its return sound larger.

Scene parameter settings make discrete changes with the engine's smoothing.
For a planned song sweep, use an `automate` lane. Positions are one-based
`@bar.beat.sixteenth`, with beats and sixteenths each from 1 to 4. The shape on
a point describes the segment arriving at that point:

```cicada
cicada 2
fx warm drive { tone = 2kHz }
track bass fm_bass { insert = warm }
pattern line { 1 . 1 5 }
scene main { bass = line }
automate warm.tone {
  @1.1.1 2kHz
  @5.1.1 8kHz smooth
}
song { main*4 }
```

Before its first point a lane contributes no value. Afterward it overrides
scene settings on that path and holds its last value. Frequency and time
parameters interpolate in logarithmic control space; this sweep's halfway
target is 4 kHz. `cicada explain score.cicada warm.tone @3` shows the
automation contribution and final target, alongside any scene setting.
The target is a prepared control value; smoothing can make the instantaneous
audio parameter lag it. Continuous lanes currently use `song` time.

## Finish and export

Write an ending into the form: remove parts, hold a final harmony, or fade
supported track levels. Master level is static; the demos use track-level
lanes for fades. Post-fader sends follow those levels, while existing reverb
and delay tails decay. Pre-fader sends keep feeding an effect through a fader
fade, which can be useful but produces a different ending.

Check the score and formatting, then render the whole arrangement before
judging one isolated loop:

```sh
cicada check main.cicada
cicada fmt --check main.cicada
cicada render main.cicada -o song.wav --bits 24 --loudness -16
```

Leaving out `--bars` renders through the end. The default three-second tail
adds decay after the musical form. Loudness targeting adjusts delivery level;
it does not repair a crowded arrangement. Compare the intro, densest section,
transition into the breakdown, return, and final tail. Inspect stems when it
is unclear which track is masking another; see [Exporting](docs/manual/exporting.md).

Use Save As before personal experiments. Small edits such as changing the
answer, moving a placement, or changing one velocity row make clearer
comparisons than replacing the entire score at once.

# docs/spec/edition-2.md

# Cicada source edition 2

Edition 2 keeps the validated language and mixer behavior of edition 1 while requiring the named mixer forms. The complete grammar is in the [EBNF appendix](docs/spec/appendix.ebnf); validation applies the edition-specific rules below. Source edition and semantic JSON format are independent: edition 2 mixer projects are represented in `cicada.project/2`.

## Selecting the edition

**Syntax:** A loose score can begin with `cicada 2`. A project selects the edition in `cicada.mod`:

```text
project sketch
cicada 2
```

**Meaning:** A loose score with no header defaults to edition 1. In a project, the manifest selects the edition; if a score also has a source header, it must match the manifest.

**Errors:** Unsupported editions and a source-header/manifest mismatch report `CICADA-VERSION`.

## Multi-file manifests

A manifest may add `entry "main.cicada"`, repeated `source "parts/voice.cicada"` directives, `license "MIT"`, and `author "Cicada contributors"`. These project directives also work in edition 1. They do not change the source grammar. Paths are explicit project-relative `.cicada` files; traversal, absolute paths, glob patterns, and escaping symlinks are rejected.

All listed files compile together. The entry loads first, followed by the remaining files in sorted path order. Source headers are optional and must match the manifest. A manifest without `entry` or `source` keeps its existing single-file behavior. See [multi-file projects](docs/spec/features.md#multi-file-projects-and-manifest-metadata) for load errors and the implemented tool support. Library imports and `cicada.sum` hash pins are supported; version requirements are not supported.

## Named mixer forms

**Syntax:** Edition 2 uses named effect declarations, named sends, per-send taps, named inserts, built-in bus declarations, and a separate mute switch:

```cicada
cicada 2
fx room delay {}
fx hall reverb {}
fx glue comp {}
bus music { insert = glue }
master { level = -1dB mute = off }
track bass fm_bass {
  level = -6dB
  mute = off
  send room = 0.25 pre
  send hall = -12dB
  insert = none
  out = music
}
pattern pulse { 1 . 1 . }
scene main { bass = pulse }
song { main }
```

The music and SFX buses exist without declarations. `bus music` may select the music compressor; `bus sfx` configures the built-in SFX bus. Track sends name a declared delay or reverb effect. A send's optional `pre` applies only to that send. Insert chains use `a -> b`. A track accepts up to eight serial inserts and the master up to 16; the music bus accepts one compressor. See [the mix chain](docs/audio/mix-chain.md). Track and master `mute` is independent of `level`.
